newsitem.title: MACAU: Macau casino tycoon Ho says violence to end soon.
newsitem.headline: Macau casino tycoon Ho says violence to end soon.

text.p: Macau casino mogul Stanley Ho has said an end is in sight to the bloody gang war that has rocked the Portuguese-run enclave for months and scared away tourists.

Speaking late on Thursday, the business leader who heads the money-spinning casino monopoly and is often labelled the most powerful man in Macau, said the confrontation between rival secret societies, or triad gangs, was almost over.
Ho spoke to reporters after a meeting of an official Sino-Portuguese group that is negotiating details of the territory's 1999 return to China.

But Ho, managing director of the Sociedade de Turismo e Diversoes de Macau (STDM), which owns Macau's gambling industry, denied he had a role in stopping the violence between rival gangs on the fringes of his nine casinos.
"Really there is no need (for my involvement). The government and the police are capable. The rain and storms of recent months will end and Macau will be peaceful," he said.
Other sources have said negotiations are under way between triad kingpins on a deal to end the warfare.
But Ho said on Friday that Macau's police force was too small to cope properly and that some elements in the force were corrupt.
"I'm afraid there're not as many people in the police as in the triads," Ho told reporters in Hong Kong.
"Police wages seem to be on the low side. So a little bit of corruption is inevitable. But this shouldn't be tolerated and the police must replace corrupt elements," Ho said.
The laid-back, picturesque enclave of Macau has been rocked this year by clashes between triad gangs, drive-by shootings, knifings, arson and bombings, killing at least 17 people.

This week a Hong Kong businessman was shot and robbed. Last week a homemade bomb was hurled at the Macau Government Palace, gunmen opened fire on a hotel injuring three security guards, and two cars were set ablaze.
Police have linked the incidents to clashes between triad gangs over illegal protection and loan-sharking rackets feeding off the legal casino business, Macau's biggest revenue earner.
Triads are secret criminal societies that operate in Macau, Hong Kong and southern China. They often are well organised and linked to a wide range of criminal activities.
China's chief representative in Macau, Wang Qiren, said last week the growing lawlessness was worrying and scolded the police for not tackling the problem vigorously enough.
Macau's government last week moved to give more powers to police and law courts to tackle organised crime.
Ho said the warning from Chinese officials and the enhanced power of the police already was having a deterrent effect and social order was apparently improving.

He also said he did not expect China to send police or troops to help tackle the triads because China could not intervene in Macau's affairs under a Sino-Portuguese agreement governing Macau's transition to Chinese rule in December 1999.
On Thursday, Macau published the names of 68 persons banned from the casinos for the next two to four years. Fifteen of them are Hong Kong residents.
Ho said the move would help the resumption of good order in Macau. "If the unwelcome people can't get in casinos, they can't do anything," he said.
A spokesman for the Macau gambling inspectorate said 1,000 people had been banned from Macau's casinos since 1988, half from Hong Kong, where triad gangs are also strong.
